body:
I think an easy solution to this would be to make the auto-duplication simply not happen if the scene that the resource is local to is the currently edited scene in the editor.

This is ideal because the edited scene is already unique - there are not multiple instances of it. The duplication is actually redundant. This solution would therefore solve this issue without affecting any existing use cases.

Let me know if I've missed anything!
@YuriSizov I know we had a discussion about instanced scenes, and correct me if I'm wrong, but as far as I can tell, the solution above wouldn't affect any of the use cases you mentioned, right?

> I know we had a discussion about instanced scenes, and correct me if I'm wrong, but as far as I can tell, the solution above wouldn't affect any of the use cases you mentioned, right?

Hmm, my use cases should be naturally safe, yes. However, I think if you instance a scene and then turn editable children on, that would be pretty much like having an inherited scene, but not at the root (I wouldn't even be surprised, if the engine follows same logic paths).

So then... One case of three, at least, is covered? I still think that this is a shared issue, so I'd prefer a solution that covers it at the core somehow, rather than patching it for just inherited scenes. I think a path to explore can be: marking auto-duplicated local resources in some way that protects them from being saved to disk with the scene. And then unmarking them if the user makes any changes via the inspector (but, crucially, not through scripts).

-----

PS. Incidentally, with instancing I actually want the opposite of what you propose: I want to avoid side effects of local-to-scene'ness when the scene is NOT the currently edited one. But as I explained, I do actually want implicit duplication to still work there, just without saving it to the owner scene and without cutting ties to the original resource. So for my use cases the solution wouldn't be as simple.

> Hmm, my use cases should be naturally safe, yes. However, I think if you instance a scene and then turn editable children on, that would be pretty much like having an inherited scene, but not at the root (I wouldn't even be surprised, if the engine follows same logic paths).

Just to clarify: I'm talking only about the *edited* scene root. i.e. `EditorInterface.get_edited_scene_root()`. I'm not talking about just any root of any instantiated scene. So the editable children are not an issue here.

The case of the edited scene root is the only case in which the auto-duplication can unambiguously be determined to be a bug, since the whole point of "local to scene" is to make something unique _per-instance_, and there is no such thing as multiple instances of the edited scene root. For all intents and purposes, the edited scene root is treated as the entire scope of all existence. This reported issue is strictly about this case, nothing else. I will edit the title to reflect this.

All other cases (such as editable children of instantiated scenes) can be debated on whether they are bugs, since one can argue that if you're instantiating, then you want the same behaviours that arise from runtime instancing. This debate lies outside of the scope of this issue. A fundamental rethinking of the local-to-scene might need to happen at some point, but I don't think of fixing this one bug as a bandaid. Also this hypothetical solution discriminates on the basis of something being the edited scene root, not on the basis of if it's in an inherited scene. As mentioned above, something being the edited scene root is very much a special case, and should be handled as such.

> All other cases (such as editable children of instantiated scenes) can be debated on whether they are bugs, since one can argue that if you're instantiating, then you want the same behaviours that arise from runtime instancing. This debate lies outside of the scope of this issue.

The bug is not with the duplication. The bug is that the implicitly duplicated resources from "local to scene" are saved as if the user has edited them. That breaks the expectation for editor context — the user doesn't want this to happen, clearly, but that doesn't remove the expectation that the editor should behave the same as runtime for the purposes of correct previews and stuff. Duplication needs to happen.

So the problem is not in duplication caused by "local to scene", and it's a shared problem for all 3 scenarios. I appreciate that you want to fix a case that is important to you without being bogged down by "the bigger picture", but you kind of open a door for the problem to be inspected and discussed here. And it would be a disservice to ignore the source of the problem for a local solution that aims to resolve your case, I think.

I do in fact have a case where your solution will be undesirable even for inherited scenes, but it involves custom resources and therefore can be brushed under the carpet as non-standard. I have resources that create canvas item RIDs of their own, for custom rendering. This means these resources cannot be shared, which is antithetical to them being resources, I know, but that's what was convenient to me. Even in inherited scenes resource instances must be unique and that deeply affects previews in the editor too.

It might be an extreme example, but it's not hard to see a simpler case where instantiation time variation is added. So I hope you will find this convincing that the problem is not with duplication, it's with serialization.

> The bug is not with the duplication. The bug is that the implicitly duplicated resources from "local to scene" are saved as if the user has edited them. That breaks the expectation for editor context — the user doesn't want this to happen, clearly, but that doesn't remove the expectation that the editor should behave the same as runtime for the purposes of correct previews and stuff. Duplication needs to happen.

The documentation says:
```
If true, the resource is duplicated for each instance of all scenes using it. At run-time, the resource can be modified in one scene without affecting other instances.
```
- The edited scene (i.e. the one open in the hierarchy) is the sole instance. What does duplication achieve?
- "without affecting other instances" - there are no other instances.

There is no correct preview that requires making duplicates of already-unique resources, since that would achieve nothing.

> So the problem is not in duplication caused by "local to scene", and it's a shared problem for all 3 scenarios. I appreciate that you want to fix a case that is important to you without being bogged down by "the bigger picture", but you kind of open a door for the problem to be inspected and discussed here. And it would be a disservice to ignore the source of the problem for a local solution that aims to resolve your case, I think.

The intent was to not over-reach and cause a bigger, more disruptive change. Hence why I'm asking for use cases that might be affected. I still don't agree that there is a shared problem, and my proposed solution doesn't rule out future changes to the other cases. I've already highlighted the distinguishing factor of the edited scene root being the sole instance in existence, and hence nullifying any concept of "duplication". The UX intent of editing a scene is to define that scene, not to instantiate one instance of that scene.

I mentioned this before, but I re-iterate that the duplication also _does not happen_ when you open up a scene that *isn't* an inherited scene. So whatever expectation exists for auto-duplication to happen in-editor clearly does not apply to _resources local to the scene you currently have open_. The fact that it happens when you open an inherited scene is due simply to systemic reasons of "well an inherited scene is just an instance with editable children, clearly". It's an implementation convenience. The UX intent of opening up an inherited scene is the exact same as opening up any other scene. The former is no more an "instance" than the latter from the user's perspective.

> I do in fact have a case where your solution will be undesirable even for inherited scenes, but it involves custom resources and therefore can be brushed under the carpet as non-standard. I have resources that create canvas item RIDs of their own, for custom rendering. This means these resources cannot be shared, which is antithetical to them being resources, I know, but that's what was convenient to me. Even in inherited scenes resource instances must be unique and that deeply affects previews in the editor too.

I'm not understanding how this would be affected by the proposed solution. Just to be clear, I want to make sure you understand that the proposed solution does not simply prevent auto-duplication within an open inherited scene. It simply prevents auto-duplication of resources _local to the open scene_. This doesn't include resources _within child nodes that are themselves instances of other scenes_. And just to be further clear, I want to make sure we are on the same page that `Local to Scene` does not duplicate resources per node that uses it. There would still only be _one_ instance of that resource within each scene instance, shared amongst all the nodes in that scene that use it.

> It might be an extreme example, but it's not hard to see a simpler case where instantiation time variation is added. So I hope you will find this convincing that the problem is not with duplication, it's with serialization.

By the time serialization happens, there is already no way to discern the original user intent. You have no idea whether something was duplicated by the user as an intentional override, or auto-duplicated.

I think we might need a specific example to talk about, because I have a feeling we are not on the same page about what the change I'm suggesting actually is.

@YuriSizov In the following examples, there are three materials involved: `bowl`, `apple`, and `banana`. Assume that all of them are marked as `Local to Scene`. Green checkmarks represent places where an auto-duplicated material is assigned by the editor. This first image shows the current editor behaviour when you open the `bowl` scene. Because the apples are instances of an `apple` scene, they _each_ receive a new instance of the `apple` material. The bananas are not instances, but are rather just local child nodes of the `bowl` scene, so they do not receive duplicates. This second image shows the current editor behaviour when you open an inherited `fancy_bowl` scene. The apple behaviour stays the same. The bowl gets a duplicate. The bananas get a duplicate, but they _share_ that duplicate, because they both belong to the same bowl instance. Please note that the auto-duplication on the bowl and bananas effectively achieved nothing, because they have not been made more unique in any way than they already were. This third image shows what I am proposing when you open the inherited `fancy_bowl` scene. Note that the checkmarks are in the exact same places as they are in the first image. Because that is the user expectation. Finally, note that none of this prevents the user from intentionally duplicating any of the materials.

@YuriSizov In showing this example, I did come to the realization that perhaps even the green checkmarks on the apples could be considered either a feature or a bug, depending on the use case, because they are also cases of involuntary overrides that get saved. On the other hand, if you want something like correct previewing, you'd want the duplication to happen. I see what you mean now when you say that it's a "serialization" issue, because I think what you mean there is exactly what I mean - that we need a way to tease out the user intent to override!

The other half of this discussion is my focus on the inconsistent behaviour that arises from the chosen implementation for inherited scenes. Because on _top_ of the ambiguous user intent in the cases that we do agree exist, I think it also introduces _more_ auto-duplications that I think should _never_ happen, because I don't think user intent regarding editor-time uniqueness will change at all depending if you are opening an inherited scene vs. a base scene. I believe it is possible to address this inconsistency as a separate aspect without delving into questions about what kinds of uniqueness there are.

@MajorMcDoom You spent too much time worrying I didn't understand your proposal, Zi :)

I really got you the first time! You propose to assume that editing an inherited scene is a special case where local resource duplication cannot have a purpose and therefore can be safely avoided. And yes, I understand that you're talking about resources belonging to _that_ scene, and not any other resource implicitly added by other scenes instanced in that scene.

And by _that_ scene you really mean the base scene of the inherited scene, because, unless modified, inherited nodes and resources do not belong to the inherited scene itself.

> I think what you mean there is exactly what I mean - that we need a way to tease out the user intent to override!

Yes, exactly. As you say, right now by serialization time we don't have a way to distinguish auto-overrides and user overrides. I believe a method can be introduced to do that, which is purely an editor enhancement (whereas changes to the way local-to-scene resources work probably involves core changes to the engine).

> I'm not understanding how this would be affected by the proposed solution.

My use case is probably hard to understand unless you work with it yourself. But to put it simply...

Consider a scripted resource that has some uniqueness created at initialization time. Not a very practical example, but say each unique _use_ of the resource should have a different color, and for some reason you need to open both the base scene and the inherited scene in the editor at the same time and see those different colors.

To account for unique _uses_ of the resource, you must mark it as local to scene. As without that, the resource will only be initialized once and all _uses_ will share the data. For this example, an inherited scene **is** a unique _use_. And that distinction may be important to the developer, albeit in rather advanced, perhaps hacky cases.

And, well, for that matter... An inherited scene can still run a tool script, it may even be the same script as the base scene. And that script may want to make runtime-like changes to the resource while in editor. But without affecting the base scene or sibling inherited scenes, and, ideally, without making these changes permanent.

So.

If, as you propose, when opening an inherited scene resources belonging to the base scene are not duplicated, these two cases are not achievable. The resources will be effectively shared between the base scene and the inherited scene, within the editor. There will be only one initialization, for one set of data, and tool scripts in both scenes will be operating on the same data. I would make a claim that this equally breaks user expectations. At least this user and his expectations 🙃 

-----

I truly believe that the core of the issue here is what is saved to disk. The biggest broken expectation is that simply instantiating or inheriting a scene causes these local resources to become unique and detach from the base scene _permanently_. And this is true for all 3 major scenarios brought up in this discussion (scene inheritance, scene instantiation, editable children).

I don't think any of your expectation would be broken if duplication still happened but, without your intervention, was never made permanent by the editor.

> This is about ensuring behavioural _consistency_ between non-inherited scenes and inherited scenes, which you are consistently reframing as me wanting to "make an exception". In my first and second screenshots, the behaviour is entirely inconsistent, because of the conveniently chosen implementation for inherited scenes. Conceptually, a "fancy bowl" should not be duplicating things any more than a plain "bowl".

I did not miss your point here. I simply disagree that what you describe is inconsistency and I've given several examples as to why duplication makes sense even for inherited scenes. An inherited scene is not the owner of these resources, it's effectively an instance of the base scene with some changes applied on top. As it is not the owner, I do no expect it to behave as an owner. I expect it to behave as an instance. And if instances, for my purposes, are supposed to not share data, neither should inherited scenes.

I'm trying to point out that you are approaching this problem from an angle that squarely fits your case, when there is a larger issue at play here. But if you insist that your problem and your case are unique and are a victim of a unique circumstance in the engine that does not share any ground with any other issue, then I'm out of words to convince you otherwise. I only injected myself to broaden your understanding of the issue in the first place. I've done that.

PS.

> I completely disagree with the framing of this as a "core engine change" in a negative sense.

When I talk about core change, I speak purely in terms of which part of the engine would require changes. With my knowledge of the codebase I would expect your suggestion to require changes to the core logic of scene instantiation, which then in turn may be utilized by the editor. I expect that some hooks would need to be introduced to prevent default behavior or branch out of it. The idea that I'm floating here can, in my mind, be isolated to the editor code only.

This is important to bring up, because core changes are usually harder to push for and get merged. It is a practical consideration, and I simply have the background to offer an opinion about that. It's not me giving it any positive or negative color.

Unless I'm missing something, for fixing this to have any breakage at all, you would need to be actively doing something in a tool script that's relying on the resource's uniqueness across multiple open scenes (in the inherited scene case) before that resource is ever touched or specifically marked as unique. For instanced scene's resources, the underlying problem still exists but is complicated more by multiple different instances being able to exist at once in the same scene.

I don't know if simply not eagerly duplicating resources in inherited scenes would be a workable short term solution, but it certainly wouldn't be for instanced scenes. I think that is reason enough to consider this worth keeping as a separate issue to the instanced scene case.
